A $3.2 Billion Fund Just Bought These 3 Stocks ©@Just_Super from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

A $3.2 billion fund opened new positions in Snowflake, TTM Technologies and Meta Platforms in the third quarter, its 13F shows.

All three stocks have fallen since Sept. 30, from 23% for Meta to 52% for TTM.

Analysts' average price targets are 51% above Meta's price and 216% above TTM's.

Snowflake is the one to buy first because its earnings estimates keep rising while its stock falls.

The third quarter's 13Fs are in, and one of the more interesting ones comes from a fund most investors have never heard of.

Tremblant Capital Group's 13F for the quarter ended Sept. 30, filed Nov. 16, shows $3.24 billion of US stocks across 62 positions. Its three biggest new positions were Snowflake (SNOW:NYSE), TTM Technologies (TTMI:NASDAQ) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ).

All three have fallen since Sept. 30. (A 13F shows only what a fund held that day, so it can't tell us what the fund paid or whether it still owns the shares.) So are they bargains now?

Snowflake's estimates keep climbing

Snowflake is the biggest of the three: 351,240 shares worth $119 million on Sept. 30, 3.7% of the fund's 13F and its third-largest holding. The stock has dropped 25% since then, even as the business keeps speeding up. Product revenue grew 37% to $1.49 billion in the quarter ended July 31, its third straight quarter of faster growth, and management credits AI products with about half of that acceleration.

Analysts have been raising their numbers all along. They expect normalized EPS to more than triple, from $1.25 in fiscal 2026 to $4.34 in fiscal 2029, and their average price target climbed from $271 a year ago to $432 now:

Snowflake (SNOW): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)

That's 69% above the stock's price, and the stock wouldn't need a higher multiple to get there. On the fiscal 2029 estimate, $432 is about 99x earnings. That's just under today's forward P/E of about 101x and well below the 130x Snowflake has averaged over the past year.

TIKR tracks 53 analysts on Snowflake. How many say "Buy"?

See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Snowflake, along with Wall Street's revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Snowflake's Analyst Ratings

The risk is that usage-based revenue can stall fast. Datadog, which also bills on usage, just guided to flat revenue from its third quarter to its fourth after its biggest customer cut back. AI work also costs Snowflake more to run: non-GAAP product gross margin slipped to 74.7% in its latest quarter from 76.4% a year earlier.

Friday, Nov 20, was a hard day for AI stocks. Nvidia fell 14.0%, a chip-stock fund (SMH) 10.6% and the Nasdaq 100 fund (QQQ) 5.7%. Microsoft fell 2.8%, less than the S&P 500 fund (SPY), which lost 3.6%.

Source: Microsoft's cash-flow statements, fiscal years ending June 30. "Left over" is cash brought in minus capital spending, buybacks and dividends. A negative "borrowed" means it repaid more debt than it took on.

Microsoft's capital spending reached $116 billion in its last fiscal year, up from $65 billion. It still paid shareholders nearly $49 billion. It also paid down $3 billion of debt. Every other big AI buyer borrowed in the year to September. Microsoft repaid. Then, on Nov. 4, it sold $25 billion of new bonds.

Its interest bill last fiscal year was $3.1 billion. That was less than the $3.3 billion it earned on its cash. The latest quarter, to September, shows the pace rising. Microsoft spent $39.4 billion against $58.0 billion brought in. We follow the other big builders' cash in Big Tech Earned $607 Billion. Where Did It Go?

Yes, about $39 billion more from its own cash.

Analysts expect sales of $396 billion in the year to June 2027, or fiscal 2027. Microsoft turns about 57 cents of every $1 of sales into cash. On those sales, that is about $224 billion.

If the AI Trade Blows Up, Meta's Saving Grace Is That Its Social Media Business Still "Generates a Ton of Cash" ©@Omar_Nasif from pixabay via Canva, @Diego Maravilla © 2022 from Diego Maravilla via Canva
Key Takeaways

Dan Niles argues Meta's ad business would keep producing cash even if the AI trade unwinds, which newly listed Anthropic can't say.

Meta's ad revenue grew 26% in the third quarter, more than double Pinterest's 12% revenue growth.

The catch is that capex topped operating cash flow last quarter, and a pullback would hit suppliers like Arista Networks first.

At about 19x forward earnings, Meta looks like a cheap way to own AI with a hedge built in.

Anthropic (ANT) closed its first day of trading on Nov. 19 at $97.17, 17% above its $83 IPO price, and Wall Street was lining it up against Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) before the shares even opened.

On the Nov. 18 episode of Squawk Pod, the day Anthropic priced its offering, CNBC senior markets commentator Mike Santoli said Anthropic's market cap "getting into the zone of a trillion and a half" makes for "a pretty clean comparison with Meta, which is at exactly that market cap."

Dan Niles, founder and portfolio manager at Niles Investment Management, pointed to the bigger difference on CNBC's Closing Bell the same day:

"If the AI trade blows up, Meta's got this other business called social media that generates a ton of cash."

Anthropic, he noted, doesn't have one.

Meta's ad business is still pulling away, too. Its ad revenue grew 26% in the third quarter, while revenue at Pinterest (PINS:NYSE), which sells into the same social ad market without a giant AI bill, grew 12%. Meta's suppliers, like Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE), would feel an AI unwind first: Arista's two largest customers, which it has identified as Microsoft and Meta, made up 42% of its 2025 revenue.

The ad engine is still compounding

Consensus has Meta's normalized EPS going from $29.68 in 2025 to $35.68 in 2027 and $42.40 in 2028, after a roughly flat 2026:

Meta Platforms (META): normalized EPS, actual and consensus estimates, $ per share, fiscal 2023-2028 (TIKR)

Prices did more of the lifting than volume last quarter: price per ad rose 14% while impressions rose 10%. Management says upgrades to its ad-ranking models are behind better conversions, and those models run on the same compute Meta is spending so heavily to build, so the AI build is already paying off inside the ad business. Meta guides fourth-quarter revenue to $73 billion to $76 billion, up 22% to 27%, while Pinterest guides to 8% to 12% growth for the same quarter.

Hank Paulson Has "Never Seen So Much Money Chasing One Opportunity." That's a Problem for Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet ©da-kuk from Getty Images Signature and CG6 Images from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Hank Paulson says too much money is chasing AI, and 52% of fund managers in Bank of America's November survey expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut within six months.

Microsoft's free cash flow has fallen two years running, while Amazon's 12-month and Alphabet's quarterly figures have turned negative.

A capex cut would save the cutting hyperscaler cash and could hurt Arista Networks if it reaches networking orders.

Hank Paulson ran the Treasury through the 2008 crisis, so when he calls a boom dangerous, I listen.

On Nov. 17, he told Semafor's Silicon Valley & The World: "I've never seen so much money chasing one opportunity with not a lot of earnings and ROI backing it up."

Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ), Amazon (AMZN:NASDAQ), Alphabet (GOOG) and Meta Platforms (META:NASDAQ) are among the biggest spenders. Meta's capex outran its operating cash in the third quarter, its first negative free cash flow quarter since 2012.

In Bank of America's November fund manager survey, 52% expect an AI hyperscaler to announce a capex cut within six months. That could hit suppliers like Arista Networks (ANET:NYSE), which has named Microsoft and Meta as its two largest customers (42% of 2025 revenue).

Follow the Cash at Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet

With revenue climbing, free cash flow is the better test of whether AI pays off.

Amazon spent $131.8 billion on capex in 2025, or 94% of its $139.5 billion of operating cash flow. Its own free cash flow measure shows a $42.4 billion outflow in the 12 months to Sept. 30.

AMZN Cash From Operations vs. Capital Expenditures: 2021-2025 (TIKR)

Microsoft's free cash flow has fallen two years running, even as revenue grew 18% in fiscal 2026, to $331.8 billion.

MSFT Free Cash Flow: FY2022-FY2026 (TIKR)

Operating cash flow rose $46.8 billion that year and cash capex rose $51.4 billion, so the whole gain went into the build-out. Analysts expect fiscal 2027's free cash flow to fall by about half, to $32.7 billion.

Alphabet's free cash flow held up in 2025, rising $0.5 billion to $73.3 billion as capex jumped to $91.4 billion from $52.5 billion. Then it turned negative: outflows widened from $5.9 billion in the June quarter to $9.1 billion in September.

GOOG Free Cash Flow: 2021-2025 (TIKR)
Demand Isn't the Issue

Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligation reached $678 billion at June 30, up 84%, and CFO Amy Hood said it grew 25% excluding OpenAI.

But a backlog turns into cash over years, and the bills come due now.
